findings.paper_title: TM Annual Performance Report FINAL
findings.headline: Forward budget risk: 2026/27 investment income expected to fall short of budget as DSG deficit reduces available cash
findings.detail: The council achieved windfall investment income of £8.2m above budget in 2025/26 (£22.475m actual vs £14.232m budgeted). However, it warns that 'interest on cash balances is less likely to be significantly higher than budgeted because of the increasing impact of the High Needs DSG deficit on the cash that the council is holding.' The 2026/27 budget assumed relatively higher returns than 2025/26, but the growing DSG deficit will reduce available cash to invest, potentially causing shortfalls against budget.
findings.matters: If investment returns fall short of the 2026/27 budget, the council will need to find alternative sources to fund planned spending, potentially requiring reserve drawdown or service cuts
findings.figures: 2025/26 investment overachievement £8.243m; budgeted £14.232m vs actual £22.475m; 2025/26 average in-house return 4.44% on £406.712m
findings.quote: Interest on cash balances is less likely to be significantly higher than budgeted because of the increasing impact of the High Needs DSG deficit on the cash that the council is holding. Relatively higher interest rates and returns than in 2025/26, were assumed when the 2026/27 budget was set.

findings.paper_title: TM Annual Performance Report FINAL
findings.headline: Elevated external borrowing rates led the council to avoid debt issuance and fund capital entirely from internal reserves
findings.detail: The council chose not to issue a green bond because 'elevated borrowing rates meant that it was not in the financial interest of the council to issue one during the year.' No new external borrowing was raised in 2025/26. All capital financing requirements were met through internal borrowing using reserves and internal balances, suggesting either cost-driven caution or balance sheet constraints.
findings.matters: A lender would be interested in whether the council is avoiding external markets due to cost concerns or reduced balance-sheet capacity, both of which could affect future borrowing costs and availability
findings.figures: New external borrowing £0m; £7m debt repaid (£2m PWLB, £5m LOBO called)
findings.quote: The council considered issuing another green bond, however elevated borrowing rates meant that it was not in the financial interest of the council to issue one during the year.

findings.paper_title: TM Annual Performance Report FINAL
findings.headline: High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £149.3m has accumulated over seven years and is creating structural cash pressure
findings.detail: The council held a negative DSG balance of £149.3m at 31 March 2026, creating an opportunity cost of £6.0m in lost investment returns during 2025/26 alone. The cumulative opportunity cost since 2019/20 is £16.4m. The council must hold reserves to cover this structural deficit, reducing the cash available for investments and other operations.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness needs to understand that a growing, multi-year structural deficit is consuming the council's resources and reducing financial flexibility
findings.figures: Negative DSG balance £149.3m; 2025/26 opportunity cost £6.0m; cumulative since 2019/20 £16.4m
findings.quote: the negative DSG balance by the end of 2025/26 was £149.3m. This created an estimated opportunity cost of £6.0m in unearned interest during 2025/26

findings.paper_title: Audit and Governance Risk management update July 2026 V1.0
findings.headline: Organisation-wide transformation delivery remains at high residual risk despite substantially effective controls.
findings.detail: The 'Delivering the Future Together' transformation programme is rated at high residual risk (16) with high inherent risk (25). Despite controls being assessed as substantially effective, the council judges transformation delivery as carrying material risk to organisational viability.
findings.matters: Large transformation programmes often fail to deliver and can constrain finances through costs and unmet savings targets; persistent high residual risk suggests delivery challenges despite management confidence.
findings.figures: Inherent risk 25 (High); residual risk 16 (High)
findings.quote: Failure to deliver organisation wide transformation

findings.paper_title: Audit and Governance Risk management update July 2026 V1.0
findings.headline: Council identifies itself as carrying high inherent risk to financial sustainability in immediate and medium term.
findings.detail: Financial Resilience is rated as high inherent risk (25) with medium residual risk (12), indicating the council recognises material exposure to financial unsustainability. The paper explicitly states this as a strategic risk: 'The council is not financially sustainable in the immediate / medium term.' Controls are assessed as substantially effective, but the underlying risk remains significant.
findings.matters: The council's own assessment that it may not be financially sustainable in the immediate or medium term is the core concern for any lender; it indicates structural financial pressures that controls have mitigated but not resolved.
findings.figures: Inherent risk 25 (High); residual risk 12 (Medium)
findings.quote: The council is not financially sustainable in the immediate / medium term

findings.paper_title: Audit and Governance Risk management update July 2026 V1.0
findings.headline: HIF1 housing infrastructure programme is subject to identified cost pressures.
findings.detail: The Housing Infrastructure Funding (HIF1) programme carries medium residual risk (12) due to programme and cost pressures. The risk poses both financial and reputational risk to the council. Controls are assessed as substantially effective but the cost pressure remains active.
findings.matters: A troubled capital scheme with cost pressures is material to lenders; capital cost overruns affect the council's balance sheet and may require external funding solutions.
findings.figures: Residual risk score 12 (Medium); inherent risk 16 (High)
findings.quote: HIF1 – Programme and cost pressures posing financial and reputation risk to the council

findings.paper_title: CA140726R17 Budget Business Planning Report - July 2026 29.06.26
findings.headline: Better Care Fund reform from 2027/28 carries unquantified risk to £32m annual pooled budget with terms still unconfirmed.
findings.detail: The government has announced reform to the Better Care Fund under its 10-Year Health Plan, but details remain unconfirmed. Any change to the council's minimum contribution level or restrictions on permitted uses of the £32m pooled budget could require significant rebalancing of adult social care provision with limited notice.
findings.matters: A £32m annual budget exposure with unconfirmed terms presents planning risk. Unexpected changes to contribution levels or permitted use could force rapid reallocation of resources at a time when the council is already under significant savings pressure.
findings.figures: £32m council share of Better Care Fund in pooled budgets
findings.quote: The Council's share of the Better Care Fund within the Pooled Budgets is £32m in 2026/27 so any change to the level of funding or the required use within that total in future years could have a significant impact on financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R17 Budget Business Planning Report - July 2026 29.06.26
findings.headline: Fair Pay Agreement for adult social care workforce (2028) presents material, unquantified cost risk with government funding shortfall acknowledged.
findings.detail: The government has announced a Fair Pay Agreement for adult social care sector workers, due for implementation in 2028, with initial national investment of £500m. The council states this funding is 'unlikely to be sufficient' to meet the required workforce enhancements, creating an unbudgeted future cost liability. Impact on Oxfordshire is not yet quantified.
findings.matters: This is a statutory obligation with insufficient central funding. As implementation approaches, the council will need to identify offsetting savings or accept higher social care costs at a time when it is already facing significant budget pressures.
findings.figures: £500m national investment; local impact unquantified
findings.quote: The implementation of the agreement presents a material and as yet unquantified cost risk for adult social care services. Information provided by national bodies indicates that the initial funding provision is unlikely to be sufficient to meet the scale of workforce enhancements needed so this is a risk that may increase future costs.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R17 Budget Business Planning Report - July 2026 29.06.26
findings.headline: Children's social care demand rising with placement cost inflation driven by insufficient market capacity.
findings.detail: Children's Services budget is increasing by £8.4m (3.6%) for 2027/28, with specific demand growth of £787k for social care driven by rising placement numbers and higher unit costs. The council identifies lack of market capacity as the constraint, meaning placement prices are being driven upward and the council has limited ability to manage costs.
findings.matters: Demand-led statutory services cannot be cut. Market-driven cost inflation in children's placements is a recurring structural pressure that will persist annually and may exceed inflation assumptions.
findings.figures: Children's Services budget increase £8.4m; demographic growth for children's social care £787k
findings.quote: Demand for children's social care continues to rise along with the cost of placements, driven by a lack of capacity in the market.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R17 Budget Business Planning Report - July 2026 29.06.26
findings.headline: High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £135.3m (net), with estimated future annual deficits of £66–79m and uncertain government support beyond 2026.
findings.detail: The High Needs DSG deficit has accumulated to £149.3m, creating a net DSG position of £135.3m after accounting for surpluses on other blocks. The council must immediately fund £13.5m (10% of the net deficit) from reserves pending SEND Reform Plan approval. Future deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28 are estimated at £66–79m annually, but the government has indicated it will not confirm support arrangements until close to March 2028.
findings.matters: This is a material, recurring liability that drains cash and reserves. Uncertainty about whether the council will fund 10% annually (£14.5m) creates planning risk and threatens financial resilience and debt serviceability.
findings.figures: £135.3m net DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026; £13.5m immediately due from council; future deficits estimated £66.3m–£78.8m annually
findings.quote: The deficit compared to Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) funding for High Needs was £56.8m in 2025/26. This has increased the cumulative deficit to £149.3m as at 31 March 2026. Combined with positive balances on other DSG blocks the overall deficit is £135.3m.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R17 Budget Business Planning Report - July 2026 29.06.26
findings.headline: Budget shortfall of £15.5m in 2027/28, rising to £22.0m in 2028/29, requiring new savings or service cuts to balance.
findings.detail: The council faces a structural budget gap driven by the Fair Funding Review 2.0 and business rates reset phased over three years. The 2027/28 shortfall must be closed through new savings to achieve a legally balanced budget by February 2027. The gap widens to £22m in 2028/29, indicating sustained structural pressure.
findings.matters: A deficit of this scale cannot be closed through reserves or one-off measures. A lender needs confidence in the council's ability to deliver £15.5m in recurring savings without service deterioration or further pressures in following years.
findings.quote: Based on assumptions in February 2026 there is a budget shortfall of £15.5m in 2027/28 increasing to £22.0m in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R16 BMMR - Revenue Update and Monitoring Report
findings.headline: New commercial property income volatility risk from Oxford Castle Quarter leasehold purchase requires creation of risk reserve
findings.detail: Following the council's acquisition of the leasehold interest in Oxford Castle Quarter, a Commercial Income Risk Reserve has been created to manage fluctuations in commercial income above the assumed £0.550m operating surplus. This indicates the council now has significant exposure to commercial property income volatility.
findings.matters: Commercial property investments create income uncertainty; underperformance against assumptions would require either reserve drawdowns or budget reductions. The need for a separate risk reserve indicates the council's awareness that commercial income is volatile.
findings.figures: £0.550m assumed annual operating surplus; £0.550m commercial income (reported in para 19 as part of £1.0m savings)
findings.quote: Following the purchase of the leasehold interest in the Castle Quarter in Oxford a risk reserve is required to hold operating surpluses above £0.550m needed to meet capital financing costs and to mitigate the impact of fluctuations in commercial income.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R16 BMMR - Revenue Update and Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Reserve drawdown of up to £2.1m approved from general balances to fund Cowley Branch Line scheme
findings.detail: The council will draw £1.9m from general balances to support the Cowley Branch Line scheme should alternative funding not be identified, with a possible additional £0.2m drawdown (total £2.1m). This reduces the effective level of discretionary reserves and represents a claim on balances for a specific capital commitment.
findings.matters: Earmarked drawdowns from balances reduce the pool of funds available for other contingencies and emergencies. At a time when contingency is tight and emerging costs are unfunded, reserve drawdowns further erode financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £1.9m confirmed drawdown; possible additional £0.2m (total up to £2.1m)
findings.quote: £1.9m held in general balances will be used to support the cost of the Cowley Branch Line should it not be possible to identify other funding for this purpose. It is possible that a further £0.2m will be needed to be added to this increasing the total contribution from balances to £2.1m.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R16 BMMR - Revenue Update and Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Cross-cutting savings of £8.7m built into budget but delivery plans not yet finalized
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes £8.7m of cross-cutting savings, but the report states that 'plans for the achievement of existing savings as well as further savings to manage the impact of funding reform and other pressures are being developed.' Detailed plans will not be shared until October 2026. This means there is execution risk on nearly £9m of savings.
findings.matters: Without finalized savings plans, there is material risk that these savings will not be achieved in full, creating a budget shortfall equivalent to the entire contingency. Achievement of these savings is essential to maintaining the forecast balanced position.
findings.figures: £8.7m cross-cutting savings in budget; £0.550m from Oxford Castle Quarter commercial income contributing to savings
findings.quote: Plans for the achievement of existing savings as well as further savings to manage the impact of funding reform and other pressures are being developed.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R16 BMMR - Revenue Update and Monitoring Report
findings.headline: £4m additional funding is one-off, falling out by 2028/29, masking underlying structural pressures
findings.detail: The council received £4m additional funding from the final local government settlement (mainly a £2.4m RSG correction for business rates pooling). However, the key component is explicitly treated as one-off funding that 'falls out by 2028/29'. This means the council will face a funding cliff and must find £4m+ of additional savings or income by 2027/28.
findings.matters: One-off funding improves the current year but does not address underlying structural deficits. The medium-term financial outlook beyond 2026/27 appears stretched, particularly given the Fair Funding Review 2.0 in 2027/28 and Local Government Reform from April 2028.
findings.figures: £4.0m additional funding; £2.4m RSG increase (one-off); falls out by 2028/29
findings.quote: The increase in RSG needs to be treated as one-off funding, as it falls out by 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R16 BMMR - Revenue Update and Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Unfunded one-off costs emerging from fire investigation and compulsory school academisations, amounts not yet quantified
findings.detail: The council will make supplementary estimates (currently unfunded) for Bicester Motion fire investigation costs and deficit school balances transferred from the forced academisation of Carterton Community College and an early years provider. The exact amounts are flagged as 'tbc' (to be confirmed), meaning these are contingent liabilities with unknown cost impact.
findings.matters: These are calls on general balances that will reduce the council's financial flexibility at a time when contingency has already been tightened. The fact that amounts are not yet known increases the uncertainty.
findings.figures: Amounts not yet quantified ('tbc')
findings.quote: Calls on balances will include supplementary estimates for the Bicester Motion fire investigation costs and to meet the cost of deficit school balances transferring to the council following the compulsory academisation of Carterton Community College and an early years provider.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R16 BMMR - Revenue Update and Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Contingency reduced to £6.2m and the council explicitly states there is less financial flexibility in 2026/27 than in prior year
findings.detail: The contingency budget was reduced from £7.3m to £6.2m as part of balancing the 2026/27 budget. The S151 officer's report states explicitly: 'there is less flexibility in 2026/27' compared to 2025/26, when service overspends could be managed. This tighter position leaves limited margin to absorb new pressures, demand shocks, or slippage in savings delivery.
findings.matters: Reduced contingency creates higher risk that small variances in demand or costs will create a budget shortfall, potentially requiring reserve drawdowns or mid-year service reductions.
findings.figures: £6.2m contingency (down from £7.3m prior year)
findings.quote: While it was possible to manage service overspends in 2025/26 with contingency measures, there is less flexibility in 2026/27. The contingency budget was reduced to £6.2m as one of the changes to balance the 2026/27 budget agreed in February 2026.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R16 BMMR - Revenue Update and Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Pay award dispute with unions expected to ballot for strike action, creating unbudgeted cost risk of up to £2m per 1% above the 3.3% offer
findings.detail: Employers offered a 3.3% pay award for 2026/27 but unions rejected it and are expected to ballot for strike action. Each additional 1% above the budgeted assumption costs approximately £2.0m. The council has budgeted £8.4m for pay inflation but actual awards remain uncertain.
findings.matters: Unresolved pay disputes create both budget risk (higher pay awards would breach budget) and operational risk (strike action could disrupt services). Additional pay costs of £2-4m would exceed the £6.2m contingency.
findings.figures: 3.3% offered and rejected; £2.0m cost per additional 1%; £8.4m pay inflation budget
findings.quote: Employers have offered a 3.3% increase in 2026/27, but this has been rejected by the unions who are expected to ballot for strike action. Each additional 1% is estimated to cost around £2.0m.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R16 BMMR - Revenue Update and Monitoring Report
findings.headline: High Needs DSG deficit of £66.3m in 2026/27 is consuming cash holdings and undermining investment income assumptions
findings.detail: The council faces a forecast High Needs DSG deficit of £66.3m in 2026/27, bringing the cumulative deficit to £215.6m. The report explicitly states that this is limiting the council's cash holdings and reducing potential investment income below what was budgeted. Deficit management is subject to DfE approval of the SEND Reform plan and receipt of the High Needs Stability Grant.
findings.matters: A £215.6m cumulative deficit represents a structural financial stress that reduces the council's financial resilience and liquidity position. Lenders need to understand whether central government support is guaranteed and sustainable.
findings.figures: £66.3m deficit forecast 2026/27; £215.6m cumulative deficit
findings.quote: Based on the SEND Reform Plan submitted to the DfE in June 2026, there is a forecast deficit of £66.3m in 2026/27. This would increase the cumulative deficit to £215.6m.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R18 Capital Programme Update Monitoring Report May 2026 (July 26)
findings.headline: Council commits £30.4m prudential borrowing to acquire Castle Quarter leasehold on forecast operating returns
findings.detail: The council completed acquisition of the Oxford Castle Quarter leasehold on 13 May 2026 for £28.5m plus £1.9m purchase costs, with additional £4m allocated for surrounding public realm improvements. The £30.4m borrowing is justified on the basis of a forecast net operating surplus of £0.5m–£0.6m per annum to cover financing costs. This is a speculative place-shaping investment dependent on successful asset management and activation.
findings.matters: This represents a material commitment of the council's prudential borrowing capacity for a real estate investment whose returns are forecast but not yet proven. If asset performance disappoints, the council will carry borrowing costs without corresponding income.
findings.figures: £28.5m purchase + £1.9m costs + £4m improvements = £34.4m total; £30.4m financed by prudential borrowing; forecast net surplus £0.5–0.6m p.a.
findings.quote: Purchase of the long leasehold interest was completed on 13 May 2026 at a price of £28.5m plus purchase costs of £1.9m. A further £4m of capital funding has been allocated to be spent on the area immediately surrounding the Castle Quarter, to help improve the street scene and drive footfall into the site. After taking account of the capital financing costs related to this borrowing there is a forecast net operating surplus of £0.5m–£0.6m per annum.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R18 Capital Programme Update Monitoring Report May 2026 (July 26)
findings.headline: Capital reserves will deplete to £36m by 2029/30, severely limiting capital flexibility
findings.detail: Capital reserves are projected to fall from approximately £230m currently to £187m by the end of 2026/27 and further to just £36m by the end of 2029/30. This rapid depletion significantly constrains the council's ability to fund schemes in advance of grants or manage timing mismatches in receipt of Section 106 contributions.
findings.matters: Capital reserves provide essential buffer for scheme advancement and timing management. At £36m, reserves will be insufficient to manage a significant adverse event, grant delay, or scheme reprofiling without triggering additional prudential borrowing.
findings.figures: Capital reserves: £230m (current) → £187m (end 2026/27) → £36m (end 2029/30)
findings.quote: The current level of capital reserves (including capital receipts and capital grants reserves) is approximately £230m. This is expected to reduce to approximately £187m at the end of 2026/27 and to £36m by the end of 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: CA140726R18 Capital Programme Update Monitoring Report May 2026 (July 26)
findings.headline: A40 HIF2 Eynsham-Wolvercote scheme at risk of missing Homes England grant funding deadline
findings.detail: Delays in land assembly and planning have put the scheme at risk of missing its grant funding deadline from Homes England. The council notes that mitigation measures are being planned and is in continuing dialogue with Homes England. If the deadline is missed, the grant funding could be lost, potentially leaving a significant funding gap.
findings.matters: Grant-funded schemes that miss deadlines often lose funding entirely, requiring the council to either abandon the scheme or find alternative funding sources. This would impact both the capital programme delivery and the council's housing infrastructure goals.
findings.figures: HIF2 scheme part of £262.7m Major Infrastructure forecast (not separately quantified), within broader £1.412.5bn ten-year programme
findings.quote: Delays around land assembly and planning mean the original programme for the A40 HIF2 Eynsham to Wolvercote is at risk of change with mitigations required to meet the grant funding deadline currently being planned. The council is in continuing dialogue with Homes England on this.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Capital Outturn Report 25-26_UPDATED FINAL (1)
findings.headline: Major infrastructure and highways projects are experiencing extended design phases, with 7 bridge schemes, HIF enabling works, and 5G projects all reporting design delays and cost/timeline impacts.
findings.detail: The Highways Asset Management Plan reports that bridge scheme delays were due to 'extended detail design phases required for a number of structures,' with 7 schemes reprofiled to 2026/27 (£4.5m). HIF projects cite 'extended enabling works' as reasons for construction rescheduling. The 5G Innovation Region programme reports 'Technical complexities on both projects requiring design changes' causing £2.5m underspend. These delays compound over time, increasing cost risk and tightening grant funding windows.
findings.matters: Design phase delays are leading indicators of cost overruns. If design takes longer than forecast, construction costs inflate and grant deadlines become tighter. Systemic design delays across multiple programmes suggest either weak project management or structural underestimation of design complexity.
findings.figures: 7 bridge schemes reprofiled (£4.5m underspend), 5G programme £2.5m underspend, HIF1 design phase extended into late 2025, multiple Stage 2 Design projects in queue
findings.quote: Bridges Annual Programme (-£4.5m) - due to extended detail design phases required for a number of structures, seven bridge schemes had to be reprofiled into 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Capital Outturn Report 25-26_UPDATED FINAL (1)
findings.headline: Two major property strategy projects—Speedwell House and Carterton Community Safety Centre—have been downsized or placed on hold due to strategic review and fire service reconfiguration.
findings.detail: Speedwell House redevelopment has been 'revised' with 'overall budget for the scheme has been reduced to reflect the revised plans' (£6.2m cut from original). Carterton Community Safety Centre is 'currently on hold' pending 'Fire Service countywide review and consideration of options on how to manage and operate the property portfolio going forwards' (£6.0m originally planned).
findings.matters: These changes signal either cost pressures forcing scope reductions or strategic uncertainty about the council's asset strategy. For a lender, this raises questions about whether the council's multi-year property and savings plans are robust or are being modified under pressure.
findings.figures: Speedwell House budget reduction £6.2m, Carterton Community Safety Centre £6.0m on hold, Property Strategy total underspend £4.5m (18%)
findings.quote: Carterton Community Safety Centre (-£6.0m) Because of the Fire Service countywide review and consideration of options on how to manage and operate the property portfolio going forwards this project is currently on hold.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Capital Outturn Report 25-26_UPDATED FINAL (1)
findings.headline: Three major school expansion projects with 720+ planned places have been reprofiled without firm completion dates: Grove Secondary, Great Western Park SEND, and Heyford Primary.
findings.detail: Grove Secondary School (600 places) was originally due February 2026 but is now planned for Summer 2026. Great Western Park SEND School (120 places) is delayed pending land transfer following consultation with no new date given. Heyford Primary is delayed due to 'prolonged planning issues for the selected school site.' Combined underspend in Pupil Places Plan was £8.1m (16% of forecast).
findings.matters: School infrastructure delivery is tied to housing-led revenue forecasts. Persistent delays in pupil place provision suggest the council cannot align capital delivery with housing growth plans, creating risk that housing development stalls or that the council faces costly emergency provision elsewhere.
findings.figures: 600 places (Grove Secondary), 120 places (Great Western Park SEND), £8.1m Pupil Places underspend, £12.2m total reduction vs original plan
findings.quote: New Grove Secondary School (-£1.4m) – the new school to create 600 pupil places is being delivered by the Education and Skills Funding Agency (ESFA) is now planned for completion in the Summer 2026 compared to the original forecast of February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Capital Outturn Report 25-26_UPDATED FINAL (1)
findings.headline: Housing Infrastructure Fund schemes are slipping towards hard grant deadlines (31 March 2028 and 31 December 2027) with explicit risk of unfunded pressure if missed.
findings.detail: The HIF1 programme spent £32.0m, £8.9m below forecast, with three major projects—Clifton Hampden Bypass, Culham River Crossing, and Didcot Science Bridge—now scheduled for construction in 2026/27. The council holds £41.3m HIF funding and £10m for A34 Lodge Hill. The report explicitly warns: 'any slippage in the grant funded elements would create an unfunded pressure' and notes the council may need to 'temporarily fund capital expenditure through prudential borrowing' if receipts do not arrive on time.
findings.matters: If these schemes slip past their grant deadline, the council loses funding or must borrow to fill the gap. With £51.3m of HIF/A34 funding dependent on delivery dates now slipping into 2026/27 or later, there is material risk of either lost grant or forced borrowing.
findings.figures: £41.3m Housing Infrastructure Funds, £10m A34 Lodge Hill grant, HIF1 deadline 31 March 2028, HIF2 deadline 31 December 2027, £8.9m HIF1 underspend in year
findings.quote: While there are other sources of funding that are expected to be used to support planned expenditure after each grant deadline any slippage in the grant funded elements would create an unfunded pressure. Progress is being monitored with updates provided through the capital governance process.

findings.paper_title: Provisional Capital Outturn Report 25-26_UPDATED FINAL (1)
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery is consistently 12–29% below forecast, with only 71% of originally planned spend reaching execution.
findings.detail: The council planned £323.7m capital spend for 2025/26 but spent only £231.3m—a £92.4m shortfall. Even the January 2026 revised forecast of £267.5m overstated the outturn by £36.2m. This 71% delivery rate mirrors 2024/25 (72%), suggesting structural inability to forecast or execute capital programs rather than one-off delays.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in the council's ability to deliver on major schemes and to manage grant deadlines. Chronic underspend suggests either overoptimistic forecasting, project management weakness, or persistent planning/delivery constraints that create risk of funding loss.
findings.figures: £323.7m original plan, £267.5m revised forecast (January 2026), £231.3m actual spend, £92.4m variation, 71% delivery rate
findings.quote: Actual capital programme expenditure for 2025/26 was £231.3m compared with £231.0m in 2024/25 and £175.9m in 2023/24... the variation between the latest programme and the actual expenditure is -£36.2m (-14%).

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Strategy and Plan 202627 FINAL
findings.headline: Internal audit resources cut by 35% to support Local Government Reorganisation, reducing coverage of business-as-usual assurance
findings.detail: The council is dedicating 35% of internal audit days to Local Government Reorganisation, leaving only 65% for business-as-usual assurance. The document states: 'To ensure internal audit capacity is available to support Local Government Reorganisation, OCC internal audit days for 2026/27 and 2027/28 have been reserved for this purpose rather than fully allocated to business‑as‑usual assurance activity.' Additionally, 'There continues to be a national challenge with the recruitment of good quality internal audit staff, particularly at a Senior /Principal Auditor level'.
findings.matters: During major organisational transformation (vesting day April 2028), reduced assurance coverage of business operations increases risk that control breakdowns in core activities go undetected. Combined with staffing constraints, this creates governance risk during a critical transition period.
findings.figures: 35% of audit days allocated to LGR; 65% for business-as-usual
findings.quote: To ensure internal audit capacity is available to support Local Government Reorganisation, OCC internal audit days for 2026/27 and 2027/28 have been reserved for this purpose rather than fully allocated to business‑as‑usual assurance activity.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Strategy and Plan 202627 FINAL
findings.headline: Housing Infrastructure Fund (HIF1) delivery phase flagged as high-risk with Strategic Risk Register listing
findings.detail: A high-priority audit of the Housing Infrastructure Fund delivery phase is scheduled for 2026/27 to 'review the arrangements for the delivery phase of the Housing Infrastructure Fund programme, providing assurance over governance, project management and financial control'. HIF is explicitly listed in the Strategic Risk Register.
findings.matters: HIF represents significant government-backed funding for housing-related infrastructure. High-risk audit classification and Strategic Risk Register listing indicate governance, delivery, or financial control concerns.
findings.figures: No figures
findings.quote: This audit will review the arrangements for the delivery phase of the Housing Infrastructure Fund programme, providing assurance over governance, project management and financial control.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Strategy and Plan 202627 FINAL
findings.headline: S106 Improvement Programme audit deferred from 2025/26; scope indicates need to improve governance and project management of developer contributions
findings.detail: An audit of the S106 Improvement Programme, originally deferred from 2025/26, is now scheduled for 2026/27. The audit will 'review the governance and project management arrangements of the S106 Improvement Programme'. S106 funds are developer contributions (Section 106 of Town and Country Planning Act) legally required to support infrastructure and mitigation.
findings.matters: S106 funds represent significant external capital contributions that must be managed and deployed according to planning agreements. An improvement programme for S106 management suggests current arrangements require enhancement.
findings.figures: No figures
findings.quote: The audit will review the governance and project management arrangements of the S106 Improvement Programme. (The audit was deferred from the 2025/26 internal audit plan)

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Strategy and Plan 202627 FINAL
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery audit deferred from 2025/26 now scheduled; scope explicitly focuses on delivery risks, delays and cost pressures
findings.detail: A Capital Programme Delivery Assurance audit, originally deferred from 2025/26, is now scheduled for 2026/27. The audit will 'review the effectiveness of delivery controls across the capital programme' and specifically assess 'how well delivery risks, delays and cost pressures are identified and addressed to provide assurance over the successful completion of capital projects'.
findings.matters: Capital project delivery delays and cost pressures are direct financial management concerns affecting council borrowing requirements and financial forecasting.
findings.figures: No figures
findings.quote: The audit will review the effectiveness of delivery controls across the capital programme, including programme management, monitoring, risk management, and reporting arrangements. It will consider how well delivery risks, delays and cost pressures are identified and addressed to provide assurance over the successful completion of capital projects. (The audit was deferred from the 2025/26 internal audit plan)

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Strategy and Plan 202627 FINAL
findings.headline: Safeguarding Transport received Red audit rating in 2025/26; follow-up audit confirms whether agreed actions were implemented
findings.detail: An audit of Safeguarding Transport in 2025/26 resulted in an overall Red rating (the lowest outcome). A follow-up audit is now scheduled for 2026/27 to 'review the effectiveness of the implementation of agreed management actions and confirm whether robust safeguarding policies and procedures are in place for the transport of children and young people via commissioned transport services'.
findings.matters: A Red audit rating signals a significant control failure in a high-risk area (children's safeguarding). The need for a follow-up audit indicates actions from the prior year's audit may not have been fully implemented, representing an unresolved control weakness.
findings.figures: Red rating = worst outcome
findings.quote: A follow up audit will be undertaken of Safeguarding Transport, which was audited during 2025/26 and had an overall conclusion of Red. The audit will review the effectiveness of the implementation of agreed management actions and confirm whether robust safeguarding policies and procedures are in place for the transport of children and young people via commissioned transport services.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Strategy and Plan 202627 FINAL
findings.headline: SEND legal challenges audit indicates ongoing litigation and decision-making control concerns
findings.detail: A high-priority audit will examine the council's control framework for managing SEND-related legal challenge 'from initial dispute through to appeal, judicial review or resolution'. The audit specifically focuses on 'the quality and oversight of decision-making, timeliness and the effectiveness of joint working between SEND and Legal Services'.
findings.matters: The existence and scope of this audit presupposes the council has experienced SEND-related legal disputes. Legal challenges can result in financial exposure, compensation liabilities, and reputational risk.
findings.figures: No figures
findings.quote: The audit will examine the effectiveness of the Council's control framework for managing SEND-related legal challenge, from initial dispute through to appeal, judicial review or resolution. It will focus on the quality and oversight of decision-making, timeliness and the effectiveness of joint working between SEND and Legal Services.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Strategy and Plan 202627 FINAL
findings.headline: SEND financial management controls being audited specifically for robustness of high-cost decision-making and forecasting
findings.detail: The council has scheduled a high-priority audit of Special Educational Needs and Disability expenditure management, focusing on 'the robustness of financial decision-making for high-cost support and the adequacy of governance, forecasting processes and oversight to manage financial risk'. SEND is flagged in the Strategic Risk Register and features as a Corporate Priority: 'Deliver more specialist school places for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND)'.
findings.matters: SEND is resource-intensive with complex funding mechanisms. The explicit audit focus on forecasting adequacy and decision-making robustness indicates the council recognises financial control risks in this material budget area.
findings.figures: No specific figures
findings.quote: The audit will review the effectiveness of arrangements to plan, control and monitor SEND expenditure, focusing on the robustness of financial decision‑making for high‑cost support and the adequacy of governance, forecasting processes and oversight to manage financial risk.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 - Draft for AG Committee 20 May 2026
findings.headline: Council forecast to use £7.3m contingency reserve in 2025/26 to manage service pressures; shift from prior year underspend position
findings.detail: The council achieved a year-end underspend of £12.8m in 2024/25 but is forecast to use £7.3m of contingency reserves in 2025/26 to manage service pressures. The statement notes there are 'some forecast overspends in 2025/26' and emphasizes 'ongoing focus on managing pressures over the short and medium term to maintain financial resilience.'
findings.matters: Movement from material underspend to contingency drawdown indicates a deteriorating budget position. Contingency reserve use in-year suggests less financial headroom to absorb unexpected pressures or service demands, which affects the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £12.8m underspend 2024/25; forecast £7.3m contingency use 2025/26
findings.quote: Control over expenditure and prudent use of contingency and other funding was demonstrated in the year end underspend of £12,8m in 2024/25 and the forecast use of contingency (£7.3m) to manage service pressures in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 - Draft for AG Committee 20 May 2026
findings.headline: Executive Director of People & Transformation departed 31 December 2025; Deputy Chief Executive roles consolidated under Section 151 Officer
findings.detail: From 1 April to 31 December 2025 the council had two Deputy Chief Executive roles. The Executive Director of People & Transformation left on 31 December 2025, after which the remaining Deputy Chief Executive (Section 151 Officer) role was updated to consolidate both financial and strategic people/transformation responsibilities under one post holder (Lorna Baxter).
findings.matters: The departure of a senior executive and subsequent role consolidation affects governance resilience. Combining Section 151 Officer responsibilities with Deputy Chief Executive duties representing strategic transformation creates significant span of control and potential single-point-of-failure risk in senior finance oversight.
findings.figures: Two Deputy Chief Executives until 31 December 2025; one thereafter
findings.quote: From 1 April 2025 until 31 December 2025 there were two Executive Director roles identified as Deputy Chief Executives; the Executive Director of People & Transformation, and the Executive Director of Resources (Section 151 Officer)... The Executive Director of People & Transformation left the council on 31 December 2025 at which point the remaining role was updated to Deputy Chief Executive (Section 151 Officer).

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 - Draft for AG Committee 20 May 2026
findings.headline: Internal audit of Safeguarding Transport received red overall rating; governance remedial action due 31 December 2026
findings.detail: Internal audit concluded that the Safeguarding Transport service received a red overall rating in 2025/26. The council has committed to establish a robust governance structure within Fleet and Transport Services, with all processes to be made transparent, well-managed, and regularly assessed for quality. Completion of this remedial action is due by 31 December 2026.
findings.matters: A red internal audit rating indicates significant control weaknesses. Fleet and transport services are critical to delivery of Adult Social Care and Children's Services; governance failures in this area could affect both service delivery and the council's ability to safeguard vulnerable users.
findings.figures: Red rating; remedial action due 31 December 2026
findings.quote: Implementation of the agreed management action plan resulting from the Internal Audit of Safeguarding Transport 2025/26 which had the overall conclusion graded as Red.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 - Draft for AG Committee 20 May 2026
findings.headline: Provisional Finance Settlement indicates over £30m in funding reductions required by 2028/29
findings.detail: The Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement for 2026/27 onwards shows that significant budget reductions totalling over £30m will be required by 2028/29. The council notes that 'uncertainty about the impact of Funding Reform / High Needs DSG deficits and Local Government Reform has made future modelling challenging' leading up to publication of the settlement. This comes alongside existing pressures in High Needs (DSG deficit) and Adult Social Care.
findings.matters: Large funding reductions over three years, combined with the current High Needs DSG deficit and constrained service areas, creates delivery risk. A lender needs to understand whether the council has credible savings plans and delivery track record, particularly given that prior audit work flagged control weaknesses.
findings.figures: £30m+ reductions required by 2028/29
findings.quote: The Provisional Local Government Settlement for 2026/27 indicates that funding reductions of over £30m will be required by 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 - Draft for AG Committee 20 May 2026
findings.headline: External audit issued disclaimed opinions on 2022/23 and 2023/24 accounts due to audit evidence gaps; 2024/25 expected to receive qualified opinion in early 2026
findings.detail: The 2022/23 accounts were delayed pending resolution of infrastructure asset valuation issues; external auditors could not obtain sufficient audit evidence and issued a disclaimed opinion. The 2023/24 accounts (published June 2024, opinion February 2025) were also disclaimed due to inability to obtain assurance over brought-forward balances. The 2024/25 accounts received positive feedback from external audit but are not expected to be signed off until early 2026.
findings.matters: Two consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions significantly undermine confidence in the reliability of financial statements. For a lender, this creates uncertainty about the actual financial position over this period. The extended path to audit sign-off also indicates resource or process challenges at the council.
findings.figures: 2022/23 and 2023/24 disclaimed; 2024/25 opinion expected early 2026
findings.quote: the council's external auditors were not able to complete the detailed audit procedures that would be needed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to issue an unmodified audit report. Therefore, the council has received a disclaimed opinion on the 2022/23 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 - Draft for AG Committee 20 May 2026
findings.headline: High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has escalated to forecast £160m with acknowledged risk of continued increase
findings.detail: The cumulative High Needs DSG deficit grew from £92.3m at 31 March 2025 to a forecast of approximately £160m by end of 2025/26, despite ongoing action through the Deficit Management Plan. The statement explicitly notes that 'continued increases in demand and inflationary pressures are proving to be considerably more significant than reductions in expenditure that can be achieved through efficiencies and demand management' and concludes 'there is therefore a significant risk that deficits will continue to increase.'
findings.matters: A DSG deficit of this scale materially impacts the council's financial resilience and balance sheet strength. While government guidance suggested central government would assume responsibility from April 2028, this remains uncertain. A lender needs confidence that the council can service debt whilst managing such a large accumulated liability.
findings.figures: £92.3m at 31 March 2025; forecast £160m at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: The cumulative High Needs DSG deficit has grown significantly from £92.3m at 31 March 2025 to a forecast of around £160m in 2025/26 despite on-going action taken through the Deficit Management Plan.

findings.paper_title: CA170326R14 High Needs DSG - March Cabinet
findings.headline: No government funding detail for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits; funding decision deferred until March 2028 statutory override ends
findings.detail: Government has provided funding detail only for deficits accrued to March 2026. No information on funding support for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits has been published. Government has committed only to confirming detail 'before the end of the statutory override in March 2028.' From 2028/29, SEND will be funded from central government DEL budget, but how that will operate is not yet specified.
findings.matters: This creates a structural planning gap. The council cannot forecast reserves with certainty beyond March 2028. Lenders and finance directors need visibility of medium-term fiscal sustainability.
findings.figures: Statutory override ends 31 March 2028
findings.quote: There are currently no further details provided on the second or third phases of the scheme to deal with deficits which accumulate in 2026/27 and 2027/28, other than to say that the Government will confirm the detail on further support before the end of the statutory override in March 2028.

findings.paper_title: CA170326R14 High Needs DSG - March Cabinet
findings.headline: Unfunded DSG balances suppressing cash reserves, costing £6.66m in unearned interest during 2025/26
findings.detail: The negative DSG balance reduces the council's usable cash position, preventing investment in interest-bearing reserves. The opportunity cost is £6.66m in lost interest in 2025/26 alone. Receipt of government grant funding in autumn 2026 could recover £1.5m–£3.0m in additional interest income in 2026/27, but this depends on interest rates.
findings.matters: While the deficit sits in an 'unusable reserve' under accounting rules, the cash impact is real. This is a hidden but material cost of the deficit and affects true financial position.
findings.figures: £6.66m opportunity cost 2025/26, £1.5m–£3.0m potential recovery in 2026/27
findings.quote: Cash balances for the year are forecast to be lower than they otherwise would be because of negative Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) balances relating to High Needs. Because this expenditure is currently unfunded it is suppressing the amount of cash balances held by the council. This will have an estimated opportunity cost of £6.66m in unearned interest during 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: CA170326R14 High Needs DSG - March Cabinet
findings.headline: Demand management not containing cost growth: exponential EHCP growth and inflation are outpacing planned efficiencies
findings.detail: The Deficit Management Plan's main mitigation is building new special school places and units (scheduled 2026–2030), but this is being outpaced by demand. The council explicitly states that demand growth and inflation are 'considerably more significant than achievable reductions in expenditure' through efficiencies and demand management.
findings.matters: If the council cannot execute demand management, it cannot control its cost base. Lenders assess execution risk; a council that cannot manage core demand is high-risk.
findings.figures: No quantified demand forecasts provided beyond deficit projections
findings.quote: Continued increases in demand and inflationary pressures are proving to be considerably more significant than achievable reductions in expenditure which can be achieved through efficiencies and demand management. There is a significant risk that deficits will continue to increase in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: CA170326R14 High Needs DSG - March Cabinet
findings.headline: Material risk: if government requires council to fund 20% of future deficits, shortfall of £13.6m–£23.4m would exceed planned reserves
findings.detail: Government has not specified what share of 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits the council will be required to fund. Current planning assumes 10%. Table 2 shows that if funding requirements increase to 20%, the council would need £38.0m (mid case) or £47.8m (worst case) over two years—exceeding the planned reserve of £24.4m by £13.6m–£23.4m.
findings.matters: This is a significant unquantified fiscal risk in the medium-term plan. The council is exposed to a potentially material funding gap if government policy changes.
findings.figures: £24.4m planned funding, £38.0m needed mid case (20% scenario), £47.8m worst case (20% scenario), £13.6m–£23.4m potential shortfall
findings.quote: The indicative amount that the council would need to fund assuming a higher residual element in both years is likely to be higher than the existing planned funding. The impact of a requirement to fund 20%, say, is also shown in the table for illustrative purposes.

findings.paper_title: CA170326R14 High Needs DSG - March Cabinet
findings.headline: Government funds 90% of historic deficit; council must fund £16.6m from reserves, plus £8m per annum towards future deficits
findings.detail: Government will provide a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of deficits accrued to end of March 2026, but the council is responsible for the remaining 10% (estimated £16.6m). The council's budget plans to add £8m per annum to a reserve (£25m held at March 2026, building to £41m by March 2028) to cover this residual and potential shortfalls in 2026/27 and 2027/28.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion reduces financial flexibility during a period of demand uncertainty. Lenders and finance directors assess whether reserves are adequate for risks.
findings.figures: £16.6m Phase 1 residual, £25.0m in reserve at 31 March 2026, £41.0m planned by 31 March 2028, £8.0m per annum contributions
findings.quote: The £25.0m funding that will be held in the reserve as at 31 March 2026 will be sufficient to meet the estimated £16.6m residual element of the Phase 1 deficit up to 31 March 2026. A further £8.0m will be added to the reserve in each of 2026/27 and 2027/28

findings.paper_title: CA170326R14 High Needs DSG - March Cabinet
findings.headline: Accumulated High Needs deficit forecast to reach £250.2m–£405.2m by March 2028, with annual overspends continuing at £83.7m–£96.1m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The £166.4m accumulated deficit at March 2026 will continue growing through 2026/27 and 2027/28. The council forecasts in-year deficits of £83.7m (mid case) and £96.1m (worst case) in 2026/27, followed by £106.0m and £142.7m respectively in 2027/28. Despite a Deficit Management Plan, demand growth is outpacing mitigation.
findings.matters: A deficit of this scale and trajectory materially impacts creditworthiness and financial sustainability. Lenders assess whether the council can control its cost base.
findings.figures: £166.4m (31 March 2026), £250.2m mid case / £262.5m worst case cumulative (31 March 2027), £356.2m mid case / £405.2m worst case (31 March 2028), £83.7m–£96.1m in-year 2026/27, £106.0m–£142.7m in-year 2027/28
findings.quote: During 2025/26 exponential growth in the number of EHCPs, and their cost, in comparison to the grant funding allocated by Government, means the forecast deficit has continued to grow despite action taken through the Deficit Management Plan agreed with the Department for Education (DfE).

findings.paper_title: 20260306R11 2025 Q4 - Oxfordshire Pension Fund Quarterly Performance Report
findings.headline: Specialist UK fibre market deterioration forcing infrastructure asset write-off
findings.detail: Gigaclear (Infracapital fibre investment) was written off after the proposed solution was rejected, driven by higher cost of capital, higher-than-expected deployment costs, and slower customer uptake. This affects the Infrastructure General Cycle 2 holdings.
findings.matters: Specific infrastructure writeoffs reduce portfolio value and highlight emerging stress in UK digital infrastructure assets where returns assumptions may have been optimistic
findings.figures: Gigaclear written off; Infrastructure General Cycle 2 shows 1.2% annualised return
findings.quote: While this has negatively impacted some of our investments, such as Infracapital's Gigaclear, which was written off after the proposed Infracapital-led solution was rejected

findings.paper_title: Section 4.6 - Earmarked Reserves and General Balances Policy Statement 2026-27 Updated
findings.headline: £2.4m drawn from reserves in 2026-27 to cover council tax income shortfall from valuation delays
findings.detail: The council is using £2.4m from the Collection Fund Risk Reserve in 2026-27 to manage a reduced tax base resulting from delays in council tax valuations in South Oxfordshire and Vale of White Horse areas. This reduces council tax income to the general fund and must be covered from finite reserves rather than operational budget.
findings.matters: Direct revenue shortfalls that must be covered from reserves rather than budget indicate pressure on the council's core funding and reduce financial resilience
findings.quote: It is proposed that £2.4m is used in 2026/27 to manage the impact of a reduced taxbase and therefore council tax income due to a delay in council tax valuations of houses in South Oxfordshire and Vale of White Horse District Council areas.

findings.paper_title: Section 4.6 - Earmarked Reserves and General Balances Policy Statement 2026-27 Updated
findings.headline: Council doubling annual High Needs DSG risk reserve contribution to £8m from 2026-27
findings.detail: In response to expectations in the Local Government Finance Settlement that councils will need to manage at least some of the historic High Needs DSG deficit, Oxfordshire is increasing its annual contribution to the Demographic Risk Reserve (renamed the High Needs DSG Deficit Risk Reserve) from £4m to £8m starting 2026-27, with the reserve projected to reach £41m by March 2028.
findings.matters: This significant annual commitment reduces resources available for other priorities and signals the council's expectation that it will need to partially fund the historic deficit itself, reducing financial flexibility
findings.figures: Contribution increased from £4m to £8m per annum; reserve to total £41.0m by 31 March 2028
findings.quote: it is proposed to increase the contribution to the Demographic Risk Reserve from £4m in 2025/26 to £8m per annum from 2026/27 onwards. This will increase the balance held in the reserve to £41.0m at 31 March 2028, when the statutory override ends.

findings.paper_title: Section 5.2 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: IFRS9 statutory override expiring 2029 will expose revenue account to pooled fund investment volatility
findings.detail: The council holds £88m in strategic pooled funds (at original purchase value; current market value £90m as at 30 November 2025). Under IFRS9, market value fluctuations normally flow through the revenue account. A statutory override currently protects against this, but it expires 31 March 2029. The council created a £5m ringfenced IFRS9 reserve in 2024/25 to mitigate impacts, but options for further reserve funding are being considered in the budget process.
findings.matters: From April 2029, any falls in market value of pooled fund holdings will impact revenue budgets directly, creating reported budget volatility. The adequacy of the £5m reserve depends on future market conditions; if markets fall significantly, the reserve may be insufficient and revenue accounts could be hit.
findings.figures: £88m original purchase value in external funds, £90m market value at 30 November 2025, £5m IFRS9 reserve created 2024/25, override expires 31 March 2029
findings.quote: The IFRS9 Statutory Override, which mandates that fluctuations in the value of pooled fund investments are taken to the balance sheet, is ending on 31 March 2029 for investments made before 1 April 2024. From 1 April 2029 fluctuations in the fund value are therefore reflected in the revenue account.

findings.paper_title: Section 5.2 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Two £5m LOBO loans with call options in 2026/27 create refinancing exposure
findings.detail: The council holds two £5m LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans callable in 2026/27. One has two call dates within the year, the other has one. At each call date the lender may change the interest rate. The council's policy is to repay if the new rate exceeds the equivalent PWLB certainty rate. This creates refinancing risk and rate exposure in the coming year.
findings.matters: LOBOs embed refinancing risk with rates set by the lender at call dates. If lenders sharply increase rates, the council must refinance elsewhere or pay the new rate. This affects debt sustainability and budget certainty.
findings.figures: Two £5m LOBOs with call options in 2026/27, LOBOs currently 7.6% of total external debt
findings.quote: The council has two £5m LOBOs with call options in 2026/27, one of which has two call options in year, with the second having a single call option in year. At each call date, the lender may choose to exercise their option to change the interest rate payable on the loan.

findings.paper_title: Section 5.2 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to increase significantly, driving strategy shift to internal borrowing
findings.detail: The council explicitly states the CFR is proposed to increase significantly over the medium term. In response, it will decrease long-term investments and increase internal borrowing (using existing cash to finance capital needs rather than external borrowing) to manage this. Internal borrowing will be limited to a combined maximum of £450m in 2026/27, with forecast internal borrowing of £295m.
findings.matters: This signals substantial capital expenditure plans ahead and represents a deliberate strategy to defer external borrowing while interest rates remain elevated. It indicates confidence in cash generation but also capital intensity in the short to medium term.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing limit £450m in 2026/27, forecast position £295m, maximum potential internal borrowing £300m
findings.quote: As the council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) is proposed to increase significantly over the medium term, the strategy will aim to decrease long term investments to allow for greater internal borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Section 5.2 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Council to borrow £65m extra for structural maintenance with £4.2m annual revenue cost
findings.detail: The council has identified a need for £65m of additional prudential borrowing specifically for structural maintenance. This will create an ongoing annual revenue commitment of £4.2m that has been incorporated into the Strategic Measures budget. This is new debt beyond the existing borrowing forecast and represents a strategic decision to bring forward maintenance funding.
findings.matters: This is material new debt creating a permanent revenue commitment. It affects future budget flexibility and increases the council's overall debt burden, which lenders will factor into credit assessments.
findings.figures: £65m borrowing, £4.2m ongoing annual revenue cost
findings.quote: Based on current forecast of balances and the proposed extra £65m borrowing for structural maintenance, the council may be required to externalise some debt from 2026/27 onwards.

findings.paper_title: Section 4.1 - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31 - V2
findings.headline: Pay inflation allocations escalate from £8.611m to £36.549m across the period, representing unallocated cost pressures
findings.detail: The MTFS shows unallocated pay inflation growing from £8.611m in 2026-27 to £36.549m by 2030-31, reaching 6.910m annually from 2028-29 onward. This represents significant employee cost pressures that must be absorbed by individual services through offsetting savings or productivity gains.
findings.matters: Escalating unallocated cost pressures indicate the council faces structural pay inflation it cannot simply pass through; services must fund this from existing budgets, adding to pressure on the structural deficit.

findings.paper_title: Section 4.1 - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31 - V2
findings.headline: Adult Services budget growing from £295.790m to £360.856m (22% increase) driven by demographic demand
findings.detail: Adult Services is the council's largest service and growing fastest, receiving Fair Funding Review 2.0 allocations of £23.233m in 2026-27 and sustained funding growth throughout the period. The £65m increase is structural and driven by aging population, not discretionary expansion.
findings.matters: Demographic-driven growth is unstoppable and structural; it will continue beyond the MTFS period and constrains the council's ability to reduce net spending, increasing dependency on external funding or service reductions elsewhere.

findings.paper_title: Section 4.1 - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31 - V2
findings.headline: Council tax increases of 4.99% planned for three consecutive years to address the shortfall
findings.detail: The council plans to raise Band D equivalent from £2,006.78 to £2,212.06 over three years, with precept increases of 6.4%, 7.3%, and 6.8% in the first three years. This sustained high tax increase is the primary visible funding strategy to close the growing budget gap, though government policy restricts how far councils can raise tax without a referendum.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether residents will sustain such high tax increases; capped increases (usually 2%) require referendums, and repeated near-cap rises signal limited tax-raising capacity to cover deficits.
findings.quote: Increase in Council Tax (precept)        6.4%       7.3%       6.8%      5.8%       5.8% and Increase in Band D Council Tax        4.99%       4.99%       4.99%      3.99%       3.99%

findings.paper_title: Section 4.1 - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31 - V2
findings.headline: Structural budget shortfall grows from £15.507m in 2027-28 to £37.241m by 2030-31 with no evident resolution
findings.detail: The MTFS explicitly labels a 'Budget Shortfall' line showing an unresolved gap that expands year-on-year. This is not a one-time problem but a structural deficit that accumulates, doubling in size over four years and suggesting the council's planned spending exceeds available funding by a growing amount.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether a council can service debt and maintain reserves when facing structural funding gaps; a shortfall that doubles in four years signals sustainability risk and reduced financial headroom.

findings.paper_title: Section 5.1 Capital Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: £35m in forward-funded schemes with specific cash flow contingency flagged on major developments
findings.detail: The council is funding approximately £35m in capital schemes before receiving the income to pay for them, using internal resources as interim financing. The s151 officer explicitly flags cash flow contingencies on two major schemes (Speedwell and Oxford Rewley Road Fire Station developments), indicating potential delays or funding gaps.
findings.matters: Advance funding creates refinancing risk and depends on internal cash reserves; delays in these flagged schemes would intensify pressure on working capital
findings.figures: £35m forward-funded schemes; contingency risk on Speedwell and Rewley Road Fire Station developments
findings.quote: This excludes any cashflow implications arising from the Speedwell and Oxford Rewley Road Fire Station developments.

findings.paper_title: Section 5.1 Capital Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Ten-year capital programme is over-programmed by £10.4m, creating delivery risk
findings.detail: Total planned capital expenditure exceeds available financing by £10.4m over the ten-year period, meaning not all schemes can be delivered as currently scheduled without additional funding, scheme deferral, or scope reduction.
findings.matters: Over-programming creates uncertainty around which schemes will actually be delivered and when, affecting service outcomes and strategic priorities
findings.figures: £10.4m overprogrammed across ten years; total programme £1,531.7m against £1,521.3m financing
findings.quote: The Capital Programme is currently over programmed over the ten - year period by £10.4m.

findings.paper_title: Section 4.5 - Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council embedded in organizational redesign through 2027/28, requiring it to plan for new unitary structure from April 2028 under significant funding uncertainty.
findings.detail: The council is undergoing significant organizational redesign planned to continue through 2027/28, including a six-month assignment of a Delivery Director to lead portfolio optimization. Simultaneously, local government reorganization is expected to create new unitary councils from 1 April 2028. The strategy emphasizes the need to plan on a 'going concern basis' and avoid short-term decisions that would damage the successor unitary council, but notes that planning for risks beyond April 2028 is challenging in a reduced funding environment.
findings.matters: Organizational change creates execution risk and absorbs management capacity. The simultaneous restructuring and LGR process increases the chance of delivery slippage against savings targets, and creates uncertainty about the new entity's financial foundation.
findings.figures: Redesign continues through 2027/28; new unitary councils operational from 1 April 2028
findings.quote: the council needs to continue to plan on a 'going concern basis.' In other words, the council should not take short terms decisions which will impact on the financial sustainability go a new unitary council/s. However, it is recognised that planning for risks/issues beyond 1 April 2028 is challenging in an environment of reduced funding.

findings.paper_title: Section 4.5 - Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Contingency budget of £7.3m deployed in 2025/26 to manage service pressures, illustrating ongoing difficulty matching spend to demand.
findings.detail: The council maintained an on-going contingency budget of £6.3m in 2026/27, but was forced to use the entire £7.3m contingency reserve in 2025/26 to manage service pressures. This suggests demand forecasts and/or savings delivery are not matching plan. General balances are being managed at a tight 5% of net operating budget (£32.6m in 2026/27).
findings.matters: Contingency depletion in-year indicates forecast accuracy or savings delivery is weak. With general balances already at the assessed minimum level, the council has little buffer for further surprises.
findings.figures: £7.3m contingency used in 2025/26 out of available amount; 2026/27 contingency £6.3m; general balances £32.6m (5% of net operating budget)
findings.quote: The use of the existing £7.3m contingency budget to help manage service pressures in 2025/26 illustrates the importance of this approach in protecting general balances and the council's financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: Section 4.5 - Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Better Care Fund £33m pooled budget subject to potential reform from 2027/28; any change to NHS-council minimum contributions could significantly impact financial sustainability.
findings.detail: The council's share of the Better Care Fund within pooled budgets is £33m in 2026/27. Government has announced 10-year health plan reform of the BCF to focus on integrated services, with details to follow. Any change to the NHS and local authority minimum contributions to pooled funding could have significant downstream impact on the council's finances, but timing and detail remain uncertain.
findings.matters: Uncertainty over £33m of funding (nearly 5% of gross spend) in a merged pooled arrangement creates planning risk. Changes could cascade through the council's financial plan with little notice.
findings.figures: £33m BCF within pooled budgets in 2026/27
findings.quote: The council's share of the Better Care Fund within the Pooled Budgets is £33m in 2026/27 so any change to the level of funding or the required use within that total in future years could have a significant impact on financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Section 4.5 - Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Children's social care costs rising faster than demand funding; market supply constraints and escalating placement costs are driving pressure.
findings.detail: The strategy identifies continuing significant pressures on demand for social care, particularly children's social care. Demand is rising and placement costs are escalating due to lack of market capacity. The government has indicated it will take action on excessive profits by children's social care providers, but implementation and local effect remain unclear. This is a demand-led service that is difficult to manage through demand reduction alone.
findings.matters: Demand-led services where costs are driven by market factors outside council control create forecast risk. If the council cannot match spend to demand, deficits emerge. This is a structural pressure that will likely persist.
findings.figures: Social care spend increased from 76% to 82% of net revenue expenditure across the council
findings.quote: Demand for children's social care continues to rise along with the cost of placements, driven by a lack of capacity in the market. While the government have indicated that they will take action to manage excessive profits by children's social care providers it is unclear how this will be implemented and what effect it will have locally.

findings.paper_title: Section 4.5 - Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council heavily dependent on council tax rises of 4.99% annually for three years to bridge funding gap; £119m of projected spending power comes from resident tax increases, not grant growth.
findings.detail: Core Spending Power is projected to increase by £94.9m from 2025/26 to 2028/29, but this assumes council tax rises of 4.99% each year (2.99% general increase plus 2.0% adult social care precept). In reality, the council faces a net reduction of £24.1m in grant and business rates funding over the period. The council tax increases are therefore compensating for grant withdrawal, not funding growth. The assumptions also include tax base growth of 1.86% annually, but actual 2026/27 growth is only 1.33% due to VOA delays in banding 2,000 new homes.
findings.matters: Dependency on maximum-allowed tax increases creates political and financial risk. Residents may resist or move house to avoid increases; bases may fall if economic conditions deteriorate. Tax base growth assumptions are also not materializing, reducing revenue below forecast.
findings.figures: £119m assumed from council tax increases over three years; 4.99% annual increase; tax base growth 1.33% actual vs 1.75% assumed
findings.quote: council tax projections for 2026/27 to 2028/29 assume that local authorities will increase their Band D council tax in line with the maximum allowable level set out by the council tax referendum principles... Core Spending Power therefore assumes that there will be further Council tax increases of 4.99% in each of the next three years paid by Oxfordshire residents which will raise £119m. The difference is a net reduction of £24.1m in grant and business rates funding from central government.

findings.paper_title: Section 4.5 - Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: DSG deficit forecast to exceed £300m by March 2028, with government support uncertain and council financial viability explicitly flagged as at risk.
findings.detail: Oxfordshire's accumulated Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is expected to reach £163m by the end of 2025/26 and could exceed £300m by the statutory override end date of 31 March 2028. The council has implemented a Deficit Reduction Plan but High Needs demand continues to outstrip grant funding growth. Government statements indicate councils may be required to contribute to managing historic deficits beyond 2028, but the extent is unclear. The strategy explicitly states this represents a considerable financial risk to council viability.
findings.matters: A £300m+ deficit in an unusable reserve, with government expecting councils to help fund it from general resources, represents an existential risk to council finances. Even if only partial responsibility falls to the council, the impact on financial resilience and borrowing capacity could be material. This is not a contingency; it is accruing liability.
findings.figures: £163m accumulated deficit forecast by 31 March 2026, forecast to exceed £300m by 31 March 2028, £70.7m annual deficit in High Needs in 2025/26
findings.quote: it is expected that the deficit on the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) Unusable Reserve will increase over the medium term and after taking account of planned mitigations could reach a deficit balance of more than £300m by the time the statutory over-ride comes to an end on 31 March 2028... This is a considerable financial risk, and if a resolution to this is not forthcoming then the financial viability of the council would need to be reconsidered.

findings.paper_title: Section 4.5 - Financial Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Out-year deficits of £15.5m in 2027/28 and £22.0m in 2028/29 with no detailed plans yet developed.
findings.detail: The council projects deficits of £15.5m in 2027/28 rising to £22.0m in 2028/29, driven by a net reduction of £27.2m in grant and business rates funding over three years from the Fair Funding Review 2.0. The council states that plans to manage these deficits will need to be developed from early 2026 onwards. The strategy indicates the council will need to assess where it is providing services above statutory minimum or above statistical neighbours and undertake benchmarking to justify service levels.
findings.matters: Out-year deficits of this scale indicate significant service reductions or income increases will be required. Lenders need to understand whether the council can credibly close these gaps through demand management and efficiency or whether service cuts will impact council tax payers and residents.
findings.figures: £15.5m deficit in 2027/28, £22.0m in 2028/29, £27.2m underlying grant reduction over three years
findings.quote: The MTFS sets out that there is a deficit of £15.5m in 2027/28 and then £22.0m in 2028/29. Plans to manage the on-going deficit from 2027/28 onwards will need to be developed from early 2026 onwards.

findings.paper_title: CC250909R10 Treasury Management Annual Performance Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Negative Dedicated Schools Grant balance of £92.5m is creating material annual opportunity costs and constraining cash flexibility
findings.detail: The council's High Needs DSG deficit reached £92.5m by end of March 2025. This ongoing liability reduces available cash for investment, creating an estimated £3.8m in unearned interest income during 2024-25 alone. The cumulative opportunity cost since 2019-20 is £10.42m, indicating this is a persistent structural funding gap that has yet to be resolved.
findings.matters: A lender assesses the council's financial flexibility and liquidity. A £92.5m unfunded liability, with £10.4m in accumulated opportunity costs over five years, signals a structural mismatch between High Needs funding and spending that materially reduces borrowing headroom and financial resilience
findings.figures: £92.5m negative DSG balance; £3.8m opportunity cost in 2024-25; £10.42m cumulative since 2019-20
findings.quote: Cash balances for the year were lower than they otherwise would be as a result of negative Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) balances relating to High Needs. The negative DSG balance by the end of 2024/25 was £92.5m. This created an estimated opportunity cost of £3.8m in unearned interest during 2024/25. The cumulative opportunity cost as a result of negative DSG balances since 2019/20 is now £10.42m.

news_drafts.headline: Forward budget risk: 2026/27 investment income expected to fall short of budget as DSG deficit reduces available cash
news_drafts.lead: If investment returns fall short of the 2026/27 budget, the council will need to find alternative sources to fund planned spending, potentially requiring reserve drawdown or service cuts

news_drafts.headline: Elevated external borrowing rates led the council to avoid debt issuance and fund capital entirely from internal reserves
news_drafts.lead: A lender would be interested in whether the council is avoiding external markets due to cost concerns or reduced balance-sheet capacity, both of which could affect future borrowing costs and availability

news_drafts.headline: High Needs Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £149.3m has accumulated over seven years and is creating structural cash pressure
news_drafts.lead: A lender assessing creditworthiness needs to understand that a growing, multi-year structural deficit is consuming the council's resources and reducing financial flexibility
